newsitem.title: SYRIA: Syrian paper urges Malta meeting to revive peace.
newsitem.headline: Syrian paper urges Malta meeting to revive peace.

text.p: An official Syrian newspaper on Tuesday urged European and Mediterranean foreign ministers meeting in Malta to help revive the stalled Middle East peace process on the original terms.

"The European and Mediterranean foreign ministers should concentrate their efforts to revive the stalemated peace process along with discussing how to advance the EU-Mediterranan partnership," the English-language daily Syria Times said.

The paper said Europeans wanted to keep the Middle East crisis in the background to concentrate on economic ties but the Arabs would urge greater European participation in the U.S-brokered peace talks.
"The Arab participants will try to call for resumed Middle East peace talks as per the Madrid terms of reference," Syria Times said.

Arabs have condemned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu who took office last June for refusing to swap occupied Arab land for peace, a principle on which the Arab-Israeli talks were based when they opened in Madrid in 1991.
Arabs also condemned Netanyahu's plans to build a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
Syria has held sporadic peace talks with Israel since 1991 but negotiations stalled over the fate of the Golan Heights, captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.
Foreign Minister Farouq al-Shara lead Syria's team to the two-day EU-Mediterranean conference, which Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy is also attending.

Officials said Shara and Levy would not meet at the Malta gathering, which is to strengthen the partnership forged between 15 European Union countries and 12 south Mediterranean partners in Barcelona 1995.
The Syria Times praised European criticism of Israeli settlement policies but said more effort was needed.
"Such efforts are still not enough as the peace process is still frozen and subject to collapsing as a result of the Israeli violations of the Madrid terms of reference and the peace agreements."
